title: Project debrief: could the desk have used this in real time?
rubric: Conclusion first: once the data are aligned on what was available, the weekly-stock 'signal' disappears and the demand–crack relationship is real but much weaker than the revised chart suggests.
Explains the five dates and uses them correctly: observation for the economics, availability for joins; release calendar with holiday delays; ingestion date useless for backfilled history.

Quantifies the stock case: week_ending join uses unpublished reports on ≈ 630 of 1,042 days and creates a −0.19 correlation; on available_at it is ≈ 0.02; the reaction is on the release day (≈ −0.53).
Quantifies the demand case: 0.83 with final data on the observation month vs 0.59 in real time; first prints revised up ≈ 145 kb/d on average; real-time growth has the wrong sign in 10 of 46 months.
Describes the safeguards: backward merge_asof on availability with tolerance and assertions; as-of views from vintages; a truncation test at several cutoffs.
Uses the vocabulary precisely: point-in-time only where vintages exist; otherwise 'pseudo point-in-time' with lags respected — and says which applies to each dataset.
States limits and next steps: daily data cannot show intraday reactions, synthetic data, few independent monthly observations; keep storing own vintages.
